newsitem.title: UK: HK stocks fall in London as world watches China.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks fall in London as world watches China.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks fell in London as traders chose to look to the UK and American markets as the rest of the world watched Britain hand over the colony to China after 156 years of rule.
With the Hong Kong market closed until Thursday to celebrate, stocks fell in London as Britain's leading shares and Wall Street chalked up substantial mark-downs.
The outlook for the rest of the week was mixed, after the blue chip Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong ended on Friday at a record closing high of 15,196.79, they said.

"We might be over the euphoria and we might see it drift back, but we still have a few more days before Hong Kong opens up, so it is difficult to say," said Barry Murrell, head of market making at HG Asia.
This week's U.S. FOMC meeting and the first budget of Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Wednesday further clouded the fate of Hong Kong stocks in London, traders said.
The Hang Seng London Reference Index ended down 79.08 points or 0.52 percent at 15,117.71, off from its lifetime high of 15,205.97.
Weaker bank stocks also weighed on shares, traders said. HSBC Holdings was quoted at HK$230.50 in London, down from its closing level of HK$233.

"We've been drifting off all day and the banks are under pressure, with the weak FTSE and weak Dow Jones," Murrell said. "There is very little turnover. I think it's just a lot of people are away this afternoon and we're drifting off with our markets."

Sharp gains in Hong Kong stocks have sparked perceptions that a flood of mainland Chinese buying was supporting the market "in order to create an aura of calm around the handover," another trader said.
That should help prices later this week and reduce the Hong Kong stock market's linkage to U.S. equity and bond markets, he said.

"There is a general feeling that the market has been propped up by flows of money from mainland China," he said. "It's less a question of the fundamental value of a company and more a guess of what China will do. I don't think they will let it collapse in the first few days of rule."
"The real challenge is as we go further into the summer," he said.

Traders in Asia said they expected the Hong Kong market to mark a new era under China on Thursday with a liquidity-driven surge as a flow of mainland money rushes into the territory to celebrate the handover.
